```{python}
#| include: false
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, cross_validate, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, roc_auc_score, root_mean_squared_error, brier_score_loss

from data2thesis import students, semesters, questionnaire, credit_data

students["employment"] = students["employment"].fillna("None")

navy = "#1d588c"
copper = "#b4762e"
soft = "#46586d"

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", font="sans-serif")
plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 150
plt.rcParams["axes.titlesize"] = 12
plt.rcParams["axes.labelsize"] = 11
plt.rcParams["figure.autolayout"] = True

f2 = lambda x: f"{x:.2f}"

true_curve = lambda x: np.sin(2 * x)
def make_points(n, seed=3):
    np.random.seed(seed)
    x = np.random.uniform(0, 3, n)
    return pd.DataFrame({"x": x, "y": true_curve(x) + np.random.normal(0, 0.3, n)})

train_points = make_points(15, seed=3)
new_points = make_points(1000, seed=4)
new_points = new_points[(new_points["x"] >= train_points["x"].min()) & (new_points["x"] <= train_points["x"].max())].iloc[:300].reset_index(drop=True)

x_grid = np.linspace(train_points["x"].min(), train_points["x"].max(), 300)
curves_dict = {}
for d in [1, 3, 12]:
    m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(d), LinearRegression()).fit(train_points[["x"]], train_points["y"])
    curves_dict[f"Degree {d}"] = m.predict(x_grid[:, None])

errors = []
for d in range(1, 13):
    m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(d), LinearRegression()).fit(train_points[["x"]], train_points["y"])
    errors.append({
        "degree": d,
        "training": root_mean_squared_error(train_points["y"], m.predict(train_points[["x"]])),
        "new_data": root_mean_squared_error(new_points["y"], m.predict(new_points[["x"]]))
    })
errors_df = pd.DataFrame(errors)

scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "student_id": questionnaire["student_id"],
    "stress": questionnaire[["stress_1", "stress_2", "stress_3", "stress_5", "stress_6"]].assign(stress_4=6 - questionnaire["stress_4"]).mean(axis=1),
    "burnout": questionnaire.filter(like="burnout_").mean(axis=1),
    "support": questionnaire.filter(like="support_").mean(axis=1),
    "satisfaction": questionnaire.filter(like="satisfaction_").mean(axis=1),
})
sem1 = semesters[semesters["semester"] == 1].drop(columns=["semester"])
dropout_data = students.merge(scores, on="student_id").merge(sem1, on="student_id").drop(columns=["student_id", "supervisor_id", "workshop", "workshop_sessions"])
X = dropout_data.drop(columns=["considering_dropout"])
y = (dropout_data["considering_dropout"] == "Yes").astype(int)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=2026)

num_cols = X.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns.tolist()
cat_cols = X.select_dtypes(exclude=[np.number]).columns.tolist()

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
    ("cat", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")), ("ohe", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore"))]), cat_cols)
])

logistic_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessor", preprocessor),
    ("classifier", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=2026))
])
logistic_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred_class = logistic_pipe.predict(X_test)
y_pred_prob = logistic_pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_class)
always_no = (y_test == 0).mean()
auc_test = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_pred_prob)

knn1_pipe = Pipeline([("preprocessor", preprocessor), ("classifier", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=1))]).fit(X_train, y_train)
knn_train = roc_auc_score(y_train, knn1_pipe.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1])
knn_test = roc_auc_score(y_test, knn1_pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=2026)
cv_res = cross_validate(logistic_pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring=["roc_auc", "accuracy"])
cv_auc_mean = cv_res["test_roc_auc"].mean()
cv_auc_se = cv_res["test_roc_auc"].std() / np.sqrt(10)

tree_pipe = Pipeline([("preprocessor", preprocessor), ("classifier", DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=2026, min_samples_leaf=10))])
grid_search = GridSearchCV(tree_pipe, param_grid={"classifier__max_depth": list(range(1, 11))}, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")
grid_search.fit(X_train, y_train)
best_depth = grid_search.best_params_["classifier__max_depth"]
auc_tree = roc_auc_score(y_test, grid_search.best_estimator_.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])
auc_lr = auc_test
```

# Introduction to Machine Learning in Python

Judged by one thing: how well it works on new cases

**Chapter 11**

Polla Fattah

---

## By the end of today you can

- tell supervised from unsupervised learning, and prediction from explanation;
- explain generalisation, overfitting, and the bias-variance trade-off;
- split data into training and test sets, and say why;
- prepare data with `ColumnTransformer`, and combine it with a model in a `Pipeline`;
- evaluate a classifier, and explain why accuracy can mislead;
- use cross-validation, tune hyperparameters with `GridSearchCV`, and run a final test.

---

## Some questions are about what will happen

- which patients are likely to be readmitted?
- which loans are likely to fail?
- which students are likely to struggle, early enough to help?

The university wants to identify at-risk students at the end of their first semester.

---

## Kinds of machine learning

| Kind | Data | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| supervised: classification | outcome is a category | considering dropout: yes or no |
| supervised: regression | outcome is a number | next semester's GPA |
| unsupervised | no outcome; find structure | clustering (Chapters 9, 14) |

Many methods are familiar statistics: logistic regression is also a classifier.

---

## Explanation and prediction

| | Explanation (Chapters 7–10) | Prediction (Chapters 11–16) |
|---|---|---|
| question | why does it happen? | what will happen for a new case? |
| judged by | sensible, well-estimated effects | accuracy on new data |
| typical models | simple, interpretable | anything that predicts well |
| main danger | confounding | overfitting |

A good predictor need not be a cause; a good explanation may predict poorly.

---

## Generalisation

Any dataset holds two things:

- the **pattern** that would appear again in new data;
- the **noise** that belongs to this sample only.

A model that learns the pattern **generalises**. One that also learns the noise **overfits**.

---

## Simulating overfitting

```python
true_curve = lambda x: np.sin(2 * x)
# 15 noisy points from a wave
train_points = make_points(15)
new_points = make_points(300)

# Polynomial models of degree 1, 3, and 12
model_d = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(d), LinearRegression())
```

15 noisy points from a wave, and three polynomials of increasing flexibility.

---

## Too simple, about right, too flexible

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.5
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9, 3.5), sharey=True)

for ax, d in zip(axes, [1, 3, 12]):
    ax.scatter(new_points["x"], new_points["y"], color="grey", alpha=0.35, s=8, label="New points")
    ax.scatter(train_points["x"], train_points["y"], color=navy, s=25, zorder=4, label="Training points")
    ax.plot(x_grid, curves_dict[f"Degree {d}"], color=copper, linewidth=1.5, label=f"Degree {d}")
    ax.set_title(f"Degree {d}")
    ax.set_ylim(-2, 2)
    ax.set_xlabel("x")

axes[0].set_ylabel("y")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The line **underfits**. Degree 3 follows the pattern. Degree 12 threads every training point and swings away from the new ones.

---

## The bias-variance trade-off

```{python}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
ax.plot(errors_df["degree"], errors_df["training"], marker="o", color="grey", linewidth=1.5, label="Training points")
ax.plot(errors_df["degree"], errors_df["new_data"], marker="o", color=copper, linewidth=1.5, label="New points")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 13))
ax.set_xlabel("Flexibility (degree)")
ax.set_ylabel("RMSE (log)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Training error keeps falling. Error on new data is lowest at degree `{python} errors_df.loc[errors_df['new_data'].idxmin(), 'degree']`, then rises.

---

## Bias and variance

| Too simple | Too flexible |
|---|---|
| high **bias** | high **variance** |
| misses part of the real pattern | follows each sample's noise |
| wrong whatever the data | changes greatly between samples |

The only way to find the model in between is to measure performance on data it did not learn from.

---

## scikit-learn designs a fair test

| Component | Module | Job |
|---|---|---|
| `train_test_split` | `sklearn.model_selection` | split the data |
| `ColumnTransformer` | `sklearn.compose` | prepare features |
| estimators (`LogisticRegression`) | `sklearn.linear_model` | specify models |
| `Pipeline` | `sklearn.pipeline` | combine preparation & model |
| `GridSearchCV` | `sklearn.model_selection` | tune hyperparameters |
| metrics (`roc_auc_score`) | `sklearn.metrics` | measure performance |

---

## The workflow of a fair test

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  A[All data] --> B[train_test_split]
  B --> C[Training data]
  B --> T[Test data, set aside]
  C --> D[ColumnTransformer] --> E[Fit and tune with<br>cross-validation] --> F[Final model]
  T --> G[Evaluate once]
  F --> G
```

All choices use the training data. The test data is used once, at the end.

---

## Use only what is known at prediction time

```python
dropout_data = (
    students
    .merge(scores, on="student_id")
    .merge(sem1, on="student_id")
    .drop(columns=["student_id", "supervisor_id", "workshop", "workshop_sessions"])
)
```

The outcome is binary ($1$ for "Yes", $0$ for "No"), making "Yes" the positive event.

The workshop came after semester 1: using it would be **data leakage**.

---

## An imbalanced outcome

```python
dropout_data["considering_dropout"].value_counts(normalize=True)
```

Only about `{python} f"{round(100 * (y == 1).mean())}%"` of students answer "Yes".

Rare outcomes are common in real prediction, from disease to fraud, and they fool anyone who judges by accuracy alone.

---

## Never judge a model on the data it learned from

```python
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=2026
)
```

`{python} len(X_train)` students to train, `{python} len(X_test)` locked away for the final test.

`stratify=y` keeps the same share of "Yes" in both partitions.

---

## Preprocessing with ColumnTransformer

```python
preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("scaler", StandardScaler())
    ]), num_cols),
    ("cat", Pipeline([
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
        ("ohe", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore"))
    ]), cat_cols)
])
```

| Pipeline Step | Job |
|---|---|
| `SimpleImputer(strategy='median')` | fills missing numbers with the median |
| `OneHotEncoder(drop='first')` | turns categories into 0/1 dummy columns |
| `StandardScaler()` | turns numbers into z-scores |

---

## Transforming features

```python
X_train_prep = preprocessor.fit_transform(X_train)
```

`fit()` estimates medians, means, and SDs from the training data; `transform()` applies them.

`gender` becomes `gender_Male`; `faculty` becomes four dummy columns.

---

## No peeking at the test data

The medians, means, and SDs come from the **training** data only.

They are applied unchanged to the test data.

Calculated from all the data, they would leak test information into the model. Packaging them in a `Pipeline` prevents this automatically.

---

## Model and pipeline

```python
logistic_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessor", preprocessor),
    ("classifier", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=2026))
])

logistic_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
```

scikit-learn specifies models with a consistent `.fit()` and `.predict()` API.

A `Pipeline` bundles preprocessing and estimation into a single atomic object.

---

## Predictions on the test students

```python
y_pred_class = logistic_pipe.predict(X_test)
y_pred_prob = logistic_pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_class)
```

Accuracy: `{python} f"{acc:.1%}"`. It sounds good.

---

## Accuracy misleads for rare outcomes

| "Model" | Accuracy | At-risk students found |
|---|---|---|
| logistic regression | `{python} f"{acc:.1%}"` | some |
| always say "No" | `{python} f"{always_no:.1%}"` | none |

A "model" that ignores every predictor scores as well or better, and helps no one.

---

## ROC AUC

The probability that, of one student who considered dropping out and one who did not, the model ranks the first higher.

```python
roc_auc_score(y_test, y_pred_prob)
```

| AUC | 0.5 | 1.0 | this model |
|---|---|---|---|
| meaning | coin toss | perfect | `{python} f2(auc_test)` |

Not fooled by imbalance. Chapter 12 goes further, including decision thresholds.

---

## Overfitting in real data: 1-nearest neighbour

```python
knn1_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessor", preprocessor),
    ("classifier", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=1))
])
```

| Data | AUC |
|---|---|
| training | `{python} f2(knn_train)` |
| test | `{python} f2(knn_test)` |

On training data each student's nearest neighbour is themselves. The model memorised; it did not learn.

---

## Comparing models without the test set

Models and settings need comparing during building.

- the training data would reward overfitting;
- the test set would be used up.

**Cross-validation** reuses the training data.

---

## Cross-validation

```{python}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
grid_data = np.zeros((5, 5))
for round_idx in range(5):
    grid_data[round_idx, round_idx] = 1

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
cmap = sns.color_palette(["#d0d0d0", navy])
sns.heatmap(grid_data, cmap=cmap, cbar=False, linewidths=2, linecolor="white", ax=ax)
ax.set_xticklabels([f"Fold {i+1}" for i in range(5)])
ax.set_yticklabels([f"Round {5-i}" for i in range(5)])
ax.set_xlabel("Fold")
ax.set_ylabel("Round")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Fit on four folds, evaluate on the fifth, rotate, average. Every student is evaluated once, by a model that never saw them.

---

## Cross-validation with scikit-learn

```python
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=2026)
cv_res = cross_validate(logistic_pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring=["roc_auc", "accuracy"])
```

Cross-validated AUC ≈ `{python} f2(cv_auc_mean)` (standard error `{python} f"{cv_auc_se:.3f}"`): an honest estimate, without touching the test set.

---

## Parameters and hyperparameters

| | Learned from data? | Example |
|---|---|---|
| parameter | yes | regression coefficients |
| hyperparameter | no, chosen beforehand | k in k-NN, tree depth, polynomial degree |

**Tuning** tries several hyperparameter values and compares them with cross-validation.

---

## Tuning a decision tree's depth

```python
tree_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessor", preprocessor),
    ("classifier", DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=2026, min_samples_leaf=10))
])

grid = GridSearchCV(tree_pipe, param_grid={"classifier__max_depth": range(1, 11)}, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")
grid.fit(X_train, y_train)
```

A tree asks yes-or-no questions in a row. Its depth controls flexibility. `GridSearchCV` searches the parameter grid.

---

## Depth against AUC

```{python}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
tuning_scores = grid_search.cv_results_["mean_test_score"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.4))
ax.plot(range(1, 11), tuning_scores, marker="o", color=navy, linewidth=1.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 11))
ax.set_xlabel("Tree depth (max_depth)")
ax.set_ylabel("Cross-validated AUC")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Depth 1 is chance; AUC rises, then levels off and dips as deep trees overfit. `best_params_` picks depth `{python} best_depth`.

---

## The final test

```python
best_tree = grid_search.best_estimator_
tree_test_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, best_tree.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])
lr_test_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, logistic_pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])
```

Evaluate once on the held-out test partition.

---

## The simple model wins

| Model | Test AUC |
|---|---|
| tuned decision tree | `{python} f2(auc_tree)` |
| logistic regression | `{python} f2(auc_lr)` |

Dropout risk rises steadily with stress and falls with support: a smooth model captures that; a tree cuts it into boxes.

Try a simple model first, and make a complex one earn its place.

---

## Predictions about people

- a student flagged by mistake may be treated differently;
- a student who is missed receives no help;
- a good overall AUC can hide unfairness to one group;
- the right use here is to offer support earlier, never to penalise.

Check the model separately for women and men, part-time and full-time students.

credit_pipe = Pipeline([

credit_pipe.fit(X_train_c, y_train_c)

## Troubleshooting guide (Part 1)

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| a near-perfect training score | overfitting; judge on new data |
| a model better than seems possible | data leakage from the future |
| high accuracy, no cases found | an imbalanced outcome |
| positive class reversed | check binary encoding (1 = positive event) |

---

## Troubleshooting guide (Part 2)

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| test set used to pick the model | it is no longer a test; use cross-validation |
| preprocessing on all the data | test information leaked; use a Pipeline |
| unequal "Yes" shares in train and test | split not stratified (`stratify=y`) |
| a complex model loses to a simple one | the pattern is smooth; that is fine |

---

## Completion checklist

- [ ] predictors are known at prediction time;
- [ ] the positive event is coded as 1;
- [ ] the split is stratified and the test set locked away;
- [ ] preparation lives in a `ColumnTransformer`;
- [ ] models are compared by cross-validation;
- [ ] hyperparameters are tuned with `GridSearchCV`;
- [ ] the test set is used once;
- [ ] AUC, not only accuracy, is reported.

---

## Misconceptions to leave behind (Part 1)

| Misconception | Better mental model |
|---|---|
| a good training fit predicts well | only new-data performance counts |
| more complex is better | flexibility adds variance |
| high accuracy means a good classifier | not for imbalanced outcomes |

---

## Misconceptions to leave behind (Part 2)

| Misconception | Better mental model |
|---|---|
| the test set can choose between models | choose by cross-validation; test once |
| a good predictor is a cause | prediction needs association only |

---

## The chapter in one sentence

> **A predictive model is only as good as its performance on data it has never seen, so design the test before you build the model.**
